description:
We’re DDE – Dedicated Designer and Engineer, a small team from Italy that loves building things where software meets hardware.

Our interests: turning open data into real, working prototypes. We work with ESP32 boards, 3D printing, DIY sensors and satellite positioning (GNSS), so NASA’s data is a perfect playground for us.
summary: SPHEREx Flipbook is a web app for exploring the infrared sky one patch and one wavelength at a time. Since 2025 NASA’s SPHEREx has mapped the whole sky every six months in 102 near-infrared colours (0.75–5 µm). That’s a huge dataset, but it’s hard for anyone outside the mission to use. With our tool you type a coordinate, a star name or a comet, and in seconds you get every SPHEREx image of that spot. You can look at it five ways: a sky map, single exposures, a blink time-lapse that finds moving objects, a spectrum built on the fly, and deep stacked images. This covers the Planet X challenge directly. Brown dwarfs, asteroids and comets give themselves away by moving between images, the same way Pluto was found. Known stars and asteroids are drawn on top, so a rediscovery can be told apart from something new. The tool checks itself against 2MASS and WISE so the numbers can be trusted. It works with a screen reader, for colour-blind users, and even by ear. That opens a brand-new NASA dataset to students, amateurs and researchers alike.
details:
What it does and how it works
One search gives you everything SPHEREx has on a target, in five views:

  • Sky: every image footprint on an Aladin Lite sky map.
  • Image: any single exposure, with quality flags, a wavelength map and the PSF.
  • Motion: exposures are combined per pass, day or visit. A template from the same wavelengths is subtracted so the stars cancel out. A PSF-matched filter then finds what’s left over, and three or more detections along a straight line at a constant rate become a “mover” candidate. Known asteroids (SkyBoT) and stars (SIMBAD, Gaia DR3) are overlaid.
  • Spectrum: PSF photometry of the target on every exposure, binned in wavelength, which builds a 0.75–5 µm spectrum while you watch. The first point shows in about 3 s, and 382 images take about 23 s.
  • Stack: deep images per detector or per spectral bin, cutting noise 5.5–8.1×. A colour mode maps water, CO₂ and CO ices and PAH where they’re detected.

You can also search for comets and asteroids by name (for example 3I/ATLAS or 2024 YR4), using orbits from JPL Horizons. A weekly watch checks your targets every 12 hours for new quick-release data and flags real changes (4–6σ) and new movers. The app also predicts when SPHEREx will next look at a position and shows where the spacecraft is right now.

Accuracy
We checked the results against independent surveys:

  • The median flux ratio of SPHEREx to 2MASS is 1.02, with 7% scatter.
  • Stacks line up with 2MASS positions to within 0.13 px.
  • Snapping to 2MASS positions and separating a neighbouring star cut the spectral scatter from 5.2 to 2.2 mJy.

We tested it on Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. WISE 0855 is a good example: its 2010 discovery position is about 2′ off by 2025, so the app moves known fast stars forward to the SPHEREx epoch.

Speed and reliability
The app never downloads whole 58 MB FITS files. It reads only the bytes it needs, in 16 parallel range requests from NASA’s AWS S3 copy, so a cutout costs a few hundred kB. When IRSA is down, it retries, then falls back to its own index of past searches and keeps reading pixels from S3.

Accessibility and creativity
Where colour is the data, colour vision decides who can use the tool:

  • There are five colour-vision modes, with palettes chosen by simulation. For deuteranopes, the smallest colour difference between bands goes from ΔE 16.8 to 31.9.
  • A daltonising filter is applied to the images.
  • Colour is never used alone: every mark also has a shape, a label or a line style.
  • The whole app works by keyboard, with a ⌘K command palette, and with a screen reader. Charts can also be shown as tables.
  • All text passes WCAG 2.2 contrast.
  • The spectrum can be heard. Wavelength becomes time and moves from the left ear to the right, brightness becomes pitch, and signal-to-noise sets the loudness.

Tools

  • Python 3.12, FastAPI, astropy, astroquery, NumPy and matplotlib on the backend.
  • React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, TanStack Query, Aladin Lite v3, d3-geo and satellite.js on the frontend.
  • The Web Audio API for the sound.
  • SQLite for caches and the watchlist.
  • One Docker image, put online through a Cloudflare Tunnel.
  • No hardware needed.

What we considered

  • Trust: everything is cross-checked against other surveys.
  • Speed on a home server.
  • Staying useful when the archive is down.
  • Accessibility from day one, enforced by a 10-point checklist in our design system that every merge has to pass.
  • Data that keeps arriving: new releases come in weekly.

Impact
Anyone can now blink SPHEREx images in seconds. Next we want shareable page links that carry the coordinates, and a way for volunteers to vote on mover candidates. That would put more eyes on new brown dwarfs, comets and nearby stars.
